entry.summary:
You might already know how to write basic SQL.
Let’s say you’ve written something like this: CREATE TABLE customers ( customer_id INT );
That’s great, you've created a table. But do you understand how it looks in the database? Is it linked to another table? What kind of data goes into that column? This is where most people get stuck - you write code, but you don’t see the full picture. That’s why tools like DbSchema include a free Community Edition, so you can learn faster by seeing how your SQL shapes the database in real time.
As you write or modify SQL code, DbSchema updates the ER diagram automatically. Instead of scrolling through raw SQL code or switching between tabs, you can see: Which table connects to which

Wanted to play around with agents. Decided to go for one of the more popular frameworks, crewai. Stubborn decided to install it local. Took me an afternoon bug fixing and library checking to get all up and working. Findings: Got down the rabbit hole in debugging, expected the issue to be in LiteLLM. Got strange errors on that one related to a module on calculation which didn't know the model name. Switched to one of the standard models, but only solved part of the problem. First tried to vibe code and vibe ask myself out of this, but unfortunately my models are not strong enough to have the mighty answer. Went back to 1999 and used good old stack overflow. Found here the answer: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65467329/server-in-a-thread-python3-9-0aiohttp-runtimeerror-cant-register-atexit-a not really related to the python version is was running nor liteLLM, but adding the # Added these two imports import concurrent.futures.thread import concurrent.futures.process
# and this is just the standard code from the liteLLM side from litellm import completion
print("start test") response = completion( model="ollama/llama2", messages = [{ "content": "Hello, how are you?","role": "user"}], api_base="http://127.0.0.1:11434" ) print(response.object) print("done test")
Going back to crewai, it worked again. Learned again a lot of stuff on vent's, python uninstall and installs. To be continued for the crewai learnings

entry.title: Meta unveils prototype VR headsets with enhanced realism and wider field of view at SIGGRAPH 2025
entry.summary:
Understanding the Big Shift in Your Google Discover Feed
First, let's clarify what Google Discover is. It's the personalized content stream you see on the Google app's homepage and on the left-most screen of many Android phones. Unlike traditional search where you type in a query, Discover proactively serves you articles, videos, and other web content based on what Google's AI believes you'll find interesting. It analyzes your search history, app usage, and location data to curate a feed just for you, making it a powerful, zero-query traffic driver for publishers. Google is rolling out a significant update that fundamentally alters the Discover experience. The platform is reportedly introducing more explicit user controls, allowing you to more easily follow specific topics or creators and more aggressively mute sources you dislike. The most notable change, however, is a major shift in content priority. The new algorithm will more heavily feature short-form video and will begin integrating a "Perspectives" tab that pulls in content from forums, social media, and Q&A sites, moving beyond traditional news publishers. For users, this means your feed will become more dynamic and varied, with a blend of professional articles and community-driven content. You'll have more power to shape it, but it may require more active curation. For content creators and SEO professionals, the ground is shifting dramatically. A strategy focused solely on traditional blog posts will no longer suffice. To remain visible, creators must embrace video and engage on community platforms like Reddit. Ultimately, this change reflects Google's broader move toward a more interactive and creator-focused internet, forcing the entire digital publishing world to adapt.

entry.title: 5 trucos para sobrevivir a tu primer trabajo como programador
entry.summary:
Empezar tu primer trabajo como programador es como entrar a un juego en modo difícil… pero sin tutorial. De repente tienes jefes, plazos, reuniones que podrían haber sido un correo y un código que no escribiste pero ahora tienes que arreglar. Aquí te dejo 5 trucos que pueden salvarte la vida (y la sanidad mental) en esos primeros meses. 1. Aprende a decir “no sé… pero lo investigo” Lo que sí pasa es que, si inventas, terminarás con más problemas que líneas de código. “No lo sé todavía, pero puedo revisarlo y darte una respuesta.” 2. Documenta TODO (aunque sea para ti mismo) “¿Y cómo rayos hice esto?” Puede ser en Notion, Google Docs o un simple archivo notas.md. Lo importante es que exista. 3. Haz preguntas inteligentes Está bien preguntar, pero evita soltar un “no funciona” sin contexto. Qué estabas intentando hacer.
Qué error exacto te salió.
Qué intentaste para solucionarlo.
4. Cuida tu salud mental y física Levántate de la silla cada hora.
Haz algo que no sea mirar pantallas en tus descansos.
No te lleves el trabajo a la cama (sí, eso incluye abrir el portátil a las 11 pm “solo para revisar algo rápido”). 5. Encuentra un mentor (o un compañero de guerra) Tener a alguien con más experiencia dispuesto a guiarte es oro puro. 💬 En resumen Si aplicas estos trucos, no solo saldrás vivo… ¡saldrás más fuerte y listo para el siguiente reto!

entry.title: Zug zug! My Claude Code now speaks Orc
entry.summary:

entry.title: Is Prompting Making Programming Obsolete?
entry.summary:
A couple years ago, I watched friends, damn good engineers, get laid off while the company announced its shiny new investments in AI tooling.
The message was clear: fewer devs, more "efficiency." Now it’s 2025, and it kind of feels like programming is… dissolving into something else. You scroll through job posts and it’s all “AI Agents,” “Prompt Engineers,” “Workflow Orchestrators.”
